How do solar eclipses affect the weather?

7 August 2026
3 minutes

As a solar eclipse is set to hit the skies next week, learn more about the impacts that such an event can have on weather – and why

By Victoria Heath

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:43
Instaread

Next Wednesday (12 August), a solar eclipse is set to occur across the Arctic Ocean, Greenland, Iceland, the Atlantic Ocean, Portugal and northern Spain. In the UK, the southwest will experience the strongest eclipse: around 90–96 per cent of the sun will be covered by the moon. Spectators in parts of Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain will see a total eclipse.

All eyes will be to the skies as the moon’s shadow passes across the Earth, but beyond the striking visual impact, the solar eclipse may play another role: in altering the planet’s weather, through cloud formation, wind speed and temperature.

By analysing the types of clouds present in the skies before and after solar eclipses, researchers at the Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute found a striking relationship between the phenomenon and weather patterns. Even partial eclipses can alter clouds: low-lying cumulus clouds – typical, fluffy clouds – dissipate, while higher-altitude clouds remain unaffected.

Clouds start to disappear around 15 to 20 minutes after the ground cools in the moon’s shadow. Once the eclipse has completed, the clouds are likely to reappear.

Other effects on weather include drops in temperature as the moon passes in front of the sun. During an eclipse in 1999, the city of Szczawnica in southern Poland experienced a temperature fall by as much as 11°C.

Because of these temperature drops, wind speeds can also become lighter and change in direction. As air cools, it becomes more dense and has greater friction with the ground. This effect makes wind slow down and turn in an anti-clockwise shift: so a south-westerly wind would become a little more southerly.

Ultimately, solar eclipses can have varied impacts on weather – but these are usually just temporary, fleeting alterations.

How can I watch the solar eclipse?

There are several ways to watch the solar eclipse next week. Tune into the Royal Observatory’s live stream from London, or if you want to see the event in-person, make sure you’re equipped with eclipse glasses. These work by blocking out the sun’s rays. Normal sunglasses are not safe to use, as they don’t provide the same UV protection as eclipse glasses.

Make sure that any eclipse glasses you purchase or borrow have the safety certification ‘ISO 12312-2′ or ‘ISO 12312-2:2015′ on the glasses.

You can also use a solar telescope at astronomy societies to see the eclipse – remember that normal telescopes without a solar filter shouldn’t be used to look at the sun.

Writer’s Reads: Andrea Wulf

7 August 2026
2 minutes

Andrea Wulf is a German-British historian and best-selling author. Read more about her top literary picks below…

Andrea Wulf is a German-British historian and best-selling author. Her latest book, The Traveller: The Revolutionary Life of George Forster and His Search for Humanity, is a biography of the pioneering naturalist and explorer George Forster.

Enjoying this article? Check out our related reads…

  • Writer’s Reads: Tharik Hussain
  • Writer’s Reads: Andrew Brooks
  • Writer’s Reads: Chiara Barzini
  • Writer’s Reads: Nicolas Niarchos
  • Writer’s Reads: Fred Pearce

Stuck on what books to read recently? Check out Wulf’s picks, from haunting novels like A Little Life to group biographies such as Jenny Uglow’s The Lunar Men.

The Alexandria Quartet (1957–1960) by Lawrence Durrell

I first read these four novels when I was 18, and I loved the way Durrell tells the same story from different perspectives.

Angle of Repose (1971) by Wallace Stegner

I fell into this novel and couldn’t stop reading. It follows Lyman Ward as he struggles to write the biography of his grandmother, who traded her glittering life in New York for the hardships of the 19th-century American West.

Entangled Life (2020) by Merlin Sheldrake

This non-fiction book about the fantastical world of fungi was an eye-opener that completely transformed my understanding of what an organism is.

Rituals (Rituelen, 1980; English translation, 1983) by Cees Nooteboom

From a masterful novelist and travel writer. This was the first of his books I read, and it made my mind soar; philosophy disguised as a novel.

The Overstory (2018) by Richard Powers

If there is one perfect climate fiction novel, it is this. Powers magnificently weaves together science, nature, poetry and humanity.

A Little Life (2015) by Hanya Yanagihara

Harrowing, haunting and utterly riveting. I read it on a long book tour in the USA and became so absorbed that I almost missed my flight while sitting at the departure gate.

The Lunar Men (2002) by Jenny Uglow

This is the book that made me fall in love with group biographies. Why tell the life of one person when you can bring to life a whole circle of people who changed the world?

The Road (2006) by Cormac McCarthy

I enjoy post-apocalyptic fiction of all kinds, but McCarthy’s sparse, dark prose and bleak landscape remain unsurpassed.
